items.item: Happens-before is the smallest relation satisfying program order within a process, a message send linked to its matching receipt, and transitivity; it is a strict partial order (irreflexive).

at.step: Reveal: happens-before, three conditions and nothing more

items.item: Two events are concurrent exactly when neither happens-before the other; concurrency is a defined third relationship, not an absence of information.

at.step: Reveal: happens-before, three conditions and nothing more

items.item: A scalar (Lamport) logical clock is a per-process counter incremented between events (IR1) and advanced past every incoming message's timestamp on receipt (IR2).

at.step: Reveal: a counter, incremented and advanced past every message it sees

items.item: The Clock Condition (a happens-before b implies C(a) is less than C(b)) follows from IR1 and IR2 and holds regardless of real clock behavior, since scalar clocks never read a physical clock.

at.step: Reveal: the same guarantee, however badly a physical clock would have disagreed

items.item: The converse of the Clock Condition does not hold: a smaller timestamp never implies happens-before, so two concurrent events can still receive comparable, meaningless-for-causality timestamps.

at.step: Reveal: the one question that single line cannot answer

items.item: Breaking ties on equal scalar timestamps with any fixed total order of process identifiers extends happens-before to a genuine total order that never contradicts it.

at.step: Reveal: a definite order for everyone, by breaking ties on who you are

items.item: The total order this construction yields is not unique; different valid clock systems satisfying the Clock Condition can yield different total orders, and only the underlying partial order is uniquely determined by the system's events.

at.deep: Internals: the three conditions and the clock condition's proof sketch

items.item: The total order can be used to solve synchronization problems such as mutual exclusion over a shared resource, because it gives every request a definite, causality-respecting place in line.

at.deep: Internals: the three conditions and the clock condition's proof sketch

items.item: Anomalous behavior occurs when the algorithm's total order disagrees with a precedence relation that exists outside the system's own observable events (Lamport's own phone-call example); this is fixed either by carrying the external precedence information into the system, or by using sufficiently well-synchronized physical clocks (the Strong Clock Condition).

at.deep: Internals: the three conditions and the clock condition's proof sketch

items.item: A scalar clock cannot detect concurrency after the fact: it compresses a partial order into a total one, which is exactly the information a vector clock preserves instead.

at.deep: Frontier: from one number to detecting concurrency

items.item: Hybrid logical clocks combine a scalar logical-clock-style counter with a physical-time component to get a monotonic, causality-respecting timestamp that also stays close to real time; this is a distinct, more recent mechanism not covered by Lamport's 1978 construction.
